subject.name: Geography
subject.description: Cambridge IGCSE Geography. Topics follow the three syllabus themes plus geographical skills (Paper 2) and investigation (Paper 4). Questions that need a map or photograph are not included yet. Written answers are self-marked against the mark scheme. The questions are original practice questions written in the style of Cambridge papers, not reproduced past paper material.

topics.title: Population dynamics
topics.summary: Population growth, birth and death rates, overpopulation and underpopulation, population policies.

topics.title: Migration
topics.summary: Causes and impacts of internal and international migration.

topics.title: Population structure
topics.summary: Population pyramids, dependency, ageing and youthful populations.

topics.title: Population density and distribution
topics.summary: Factors affecting where people live.

topics.title: Settlements and service provision
topics.summary: Settlement sites, hierarchy, services, threshold and range.

topics.title: Urban settlements
topics.summary: Urban land use, problems and solutions.

topics.title: Urbanisation
topics.summary: Rapid urban growth and its impacts; squatter settlements.

topics.title: Earthquakes and volcanoes
topics.summary: Plate tectonics, hazards and responses.

topics.title: Rivers
topics.summary: River processes, landforms, hazards and management.

topics.title: Coasts
topics.summary: Coastal processes, landforms, coral reefs, mangroves and management.

topics.title: Weather
topics.summary: Measuring and recording weather.

topics.title: Climate and natural vegetation
topics.summary: Equatorial and hot desert climates and ecosystems.

topics.title: Development
topics.summary: Indicators, inequality, globalisation and TNCs.

topics.title: Food production
topics.summary: Farming systems, food shortages and solutions.

topics.title: Industry
topics.summary: Industrial systems and location factors.

topics.title: Tourism
topics.summary: Growth, impacts and management of tourism.

topics.title: Energy
topics.summary: Energy sources, supply and demand.

topics.title: Water
topics.summary: Water supply, demand and management.

topics.title: Environmental risks of economic development
topics.summary: Pollution, climate change, deforestation and conservation.

topics.title: Map skills
topics.summary: Grid references, scale, distance, direction and relief on topographic maps.

topics.title: Graphs and data
topics.summary: Reading, drawing and interpreting graphs, tables and statistics.

topics.title: Geographical investigation
topics.summary: Hypotheses, fieldwork methods, presenting and evaluating data.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define natural increase.

markingPoints.text: birth rate minus death rate
the growth (or decline) of a population excluding migration

parts.examinerComment: Many omitted the reference to migration.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A country has a birth rate of {b} per 1000 and a death rate of {d} per 1000. Calculate its natural increase, per 1000.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=b-d} per 1000

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why birth rates usually fall as countries develop.

markingPoints.text: better access to contraception / family planning
more women are educated and have careers, so marry and have children later
lower infant mortality, so fewer births are needed to ensure children survive
children are expensive in urban areas and are no longer needed to work on farms
developed point: e.g. pensions reduce the need for children to support parents in old age

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers explained why each factor reduces births instead of just listing factors.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between voluntary and forced migration.

markingPoints.text: voluntary: people choose to move, e.g. for work
forced: people have no choice, e.g. because of war or natural disaster

parts.examinerComment: Examples help show understanding.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give two push factors that cause people to leave rural areas.

markingPoints.text: lack of jobs / low wages
poor services, e.g. schools or healthcare
crop failure / drought
conflict

parts.examinerComment: Pull factors were credited only if phrased as push factors.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain two impacts of out-migration on the area people leave.

markingPoints.text: loss of young, economically active people
leaves an ageing population / fewer workers for farms
remittances sent home increase incomes
less pressure on land and resources
'brain drain' of skilled workers

parts.examinerComment: Both positive and negative impacts were credited.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: What does a wide base on a population pyramid show?

markingPoints.text: a high birth rate / a large proportion of young people

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A country has {dep} dependants for every {w} people of working age. Calculate the dependency ratio (dependants ÷ working population × 100).

markingPoints.text: M1 for {dep} ÷ {w} × 100
A1 for {=round(dep/w*100, 1)}

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates divided the wrong way round. The working population goes on the bottom.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain the problems an ageing population can cause for a country.

markingPoints.text: higher costs of pensions
greater demand for healthcare and care homes
fewer workers, so a smaller tax base
labour shortages may slow economic growth
developed point linking cause and effect

parts.examinerComment: Answers should explain why each is a problem.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A region has {p} million people living in an area of {a} km². Calculate its population density, in people per km².
parts.examinerComment: Converting millions correctly was essential.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give two physical factors that can cause low population density.

markingPoints.text: extreme climate (very hot, cold or dry)
mountainous or steep relief
poor soils
dense vegetation, e.g. rainforest

parts.examinerComment: Human factors such as lack of jobs were not credited.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why river valleys and coastal plains are often densely populated.

markingPoints.text: flat land for building and farming
fertile soils / water supply for farming
easy transport and trade routes
access to ports and fishing

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define the sphere of influence of a settlement.

markingPoints.text: the area served by a settlement / from which people travel to use its services

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: What is a low-order service? Give one example.

markingPoints.text: a service used frequently, with a small threshold and range
e.g. a newsagent, bakery or primary school

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why larger settlements provide more high-order services.

markingPoints.text: high-order services need a large threshold population
larger settlements have more people / a larger sphere of influence
people will travel further (a larger range) for high-order goods

parts.examinerComment: Use the terms threshold and range.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name the zone of a city that contains most shops and offices.

markingPoints.text: CBD / central business district

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe two characteristics of the rural–urban fringe.

markingPoints.text: mix of urban and rural land uses
new housing estates / out-of-town retail parks / business parks
lower building density, more open space

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain the causes of traffic congestion in the CBD and describe one solution.

markingPoints.text: many people commute into the CBD for work and shopping
narrow, old street patterns
rush hour peaks
solution, e.g. park-and-ride, congestion charging, improved public transport
explains how the solution reduces traffic

parts.examinerComment: Solutions needed explaining, not just naming.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define urbanisation.

markingPoints.text: an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas

parts.examinerComment: Growth in the number of people alone is urban growth, not urbanisation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give two characteristics of squatter settlements.

markingPoints.text: built illegally on land not owned by residents
homes made from scrap materials
lack of clean water, sanitation or electricity
overcrowded

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain two strategies used to improve squatter settlements.

markingPoints.text: self-help schemes: residents given materials to improve homes
site-and-service schemes provide plots with water and sanitation
legal land rights encourage residents to invest
installation of water pipes, drains and electricity
developed explanation of benefit

parts.examinerComment: Each strategy needs an explanation of how it improves living conditions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name the type of plate boundary where plates move apart.

markingPoints.text: constructive / divergent

parts.examinerComment: Destructive boundaries are where plates move together.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which scale is used to measure the magnitude of an earthquake?

markingPoints.text: C – Richter (or moment magnitude) scale

parts.examinerComment: The Mercalli scale measures effects (intensity), not magnitude.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why people continue to live near active volcanoes.

markingPoints.text: fertile volcanic soils for farming
tourism provides jobs and income
geothermal energy
minerals for mining
eruptions are infrequent / can be monitored and predicted

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name the transport process in which minerals are carried dissolved in the river water.

markingPoints.text: solution

parts.examinerComment: Suspension, saltation and traction carry solid particles.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe how a waterfall forms.

markingPoints.text: band of hard rock overlying softer rock
soft rock is eroded faster, creating an overhang
overhang collapses
plunge pool deepened by hydraulic action and abrasion
waterfall retreats upstream forming a gorge

parts.examinerComment: Sequence matters. A labelled sketch can help.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State two features of a river's lower course.

markingPoints.text: wide, deep channel
floodplain
meanders / ox-bow lakes
levées
delta or estuary

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which process moves sediment along a coastline?

markingPoints.text: C – longshore drift

parts.examinerComment: Abrasion and attrition are processes of erosion.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe how a spit forms.

markingPoints.text: longshore drift transports sediment along the coast
where the coastline changes direction, deposition occurs
sediment builds up to form a ridge extending into the sea
wind or waves curve the end (recurved hook)
salt marsh forms behind it

parts.examinerComment: Well answered by those who referred to a change in coastline direction.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Name two methods of hard engineering used to protect coastlines.

markingPoints.text: sea walls
groynes
rock armour (rip-rap)
gabions

parts.examinerComment: Beach nourishment is soft engineering.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name the instrument used to measure air pressure.

markingPoints.text: barometer

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: On one day the maximum temperature was {mx} °C and the minimum was {mn} °C. Calculate the daily temperature range, in °C.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=mx-mn}

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why a Stevenson screen is painted white and raised above the ground.

markingPoints.text: white reflects the Sun's rays so readings show air temperature, not direct heating
raised (about 1.2 m) to avoid heat from the ground

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which climate has high temperatures and high rainfall throughout the year?

markingPoints.text: A – equatorial

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe two ways in which tropical rainforest plants are adapted to their environment.

markingPoints.text: drip-tip leaves shed heavy rainfall
buttress roots support tall trees in shallow soils
lianas climb to reach light
epiphytes grow on branches to reach light

parts.examinerComment: Each adaptation should be linked to the condition it suits.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why hot deserts have a large daily temperature range.

markingPoints.text: clear skies / little cloud cover
strong heating by the Sun during the day
heat is lost rapidly at night by radiation, with no cloud to trap it

parts.examinerComment: Many mentioned clear skies but did not explain the night-time effect.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name one indicator of development.

markingPoints.text: e.g. GNI per capita, HDI, life expectancy, literacy rate, infant mortality

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the Human Development Index (HDI) is a better measure of development than GNI per capita alone.

markingPoints.text: HDI combines several indicators: health, education and income
GNI per capita is an average that ignores inequality and quality of life

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how a transnational corporation (TNC) can benefit a host country.

markingPoints.text: creates jobs
brings investment and improved infrastructure
increases tax revenue for the government
transfer of skills and technology
developed point linking a benefit to development

parts.examinerComment: Answers should be about the host country, not the TNC.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between commercial and subsistence farming.

markingPoints.text: commercial farming produces crops or livestock for sale / profit
subsistence farming produces food for the farmer's family

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe two causes of food shortages.

markingPoints.text: drought or flooding
pests and diseases
conflict
soil erosion / exhaustion
poverty / lack of investment

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how irrigation can increase crop yields, and describe one problem it may cause.

markingPoints.text: provides water when rainfall is low or unreliable
allows more than one crop per year / growing in dry areas
problem: salinisation or waterlogging of soils / falling water tables

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: To which sector of industry does car manufacturing belong?

markingPoints.text: B – secondary

parts.examinerComment: Secondary industry processes raw materials into products.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give two factors that influence the location of a factory.

markingPoints.text: raw materials
labour supply
transport links
market
government incentives
cheap, flat land

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why high-technology industries often locate near universities.

markingPoints.text: access to research and development
supply of highly skilled graduates
opportunities to work with researchers / science parks

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Give two physical attractions for tourists.

markingPoints.text: beaches
mountains / scenery
warm, sunny climate
wildlife

parts.examinerComment: Human attractions such as museums were not credited.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how tourism can benefit a local economy.

markingPoints.text: creates jobs, e.g. in hotels
multiplier effect: money spent supports other businesses
improves infrastructure
foreign currency

parts.examinerComment: The best answers explained the multiplier effect.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe one strategy for making tourism more sustainable.

markingPoints.text: e.g. ecotourism / limiting visitor numbers / using local staff and produce
explains how it protects the environment or benefits local people

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which energy source is renewable?

markingPoints.text: D – wind

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give two advantages of hydro-electric power (HEP).

markingPoints.text: renewable
no greenhouse gas emissions during operation
reservoir can provide water supply / flood control
reliable output

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain the disadvantages of nuclear power.

markingPoints.text: radioactive waste is dangerous and difficult to store
risk of accidents releasing radiation
high cost of building and decommissioning
uranium is finite

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State two uses of water in low-income countries.

markingPoints.text: domestic use: drinking, cooking, washing
irrigation for farming
industry

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how building a dam and reservoir can increase water supply.

markingPoints.text: stores water during wet periods
so it can be released during dry periods / to cities and farms

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe one way in which polluted water affects human health.

markingPoints.text: spreads waterborne diseases such as cholera or typhoid
causes diarrhoea / dehydration, especially in children

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name two consequences of deforestation.

markingPoints.text: loss of biodiversity / habitats
soil erosion
increased flooding
more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how burning fossil fuels may contribute to climate change.

markingPoints.text: releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas)
enhances the greenhouse effect: more heat is trapped in the atmosphere
global temperatures rise

parts.examinerComment: Confusing climate change with the ozone layer was a common error.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe one strategy to reduce the environmental impact of economic development.

markingPoints.text: e.g. renewable energy, reforestation, protected areas, pollution laws
explains how it reduces the impact

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: On a 1 : 50 000 map, two points are {c} cm apart. Calculate the real distance between them, in km.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=c*0.5} km

parts.examinerComment: Converting cm to km was the main source of error.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A point lies three-tenths of the way east from easting 45 and seven-tenths of the way north from northing 21. Give its six-figure grid reference.
parts.examinerComment: Eastings come before northings: 'along the corridor and up the stairs'.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: On a map, what do contour lines that are very close together show?

markingPoints.text: C – a steep slope

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Monthly rainfall from January to June was {r1}, {r2}, {r3}, {r4}, {r5} and {r6} mm. Calculate the total rainfall for these six months, in mm.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=r1+r2+r3+r4+r5+r6}

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean of these temperatures: {t1}, {t2}, {t3} and {t4} °C.
parts.examinerComment: Add all four values and divide by four; a common error was dividing by three.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Which type of graph is best for showing the percentage share of different land uses?

markingPoints.text: B – pie chart

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

questions.stem: Fig. 1 is a climate graph for a location in the tropics.

figures.alt: Climate graph for a tropical location. Monthly temperatures range from 24 °C in December and January to 31 °C in April. Rainfall is very low from November to March and highest in June at 260 mm.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the annual temperature range, in °C.

markingPoints.text: M1 for 31 − 24
A1 for 7 °C

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Name the wettest month.

markingPoints.text: June

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe the pattern of rainfall shown in Fig. 1.

markingPoints.text: a distinct wet season and dry season
wet season from about April/May to September, peaking at 260 mm in June
dry season from November to March with under 50 mm per month

parts.examinerComment: Use figures from the graph to support your description.

questions.stem: Fig. 2 is a population pyramid for a country.

figures.alt: Population pyramid with a wide base narrowing sharply with age. Ages 0–14: 21% male, 20% female. Ages 75+: 0.5% male, 0.5% female.
figures.caption: Fig. 2

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: What percentage of the total population is aged 0–14?

markingPoints.text: B1 for 41%

parts.examinerComment: Both sides of the pyramid must be added.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Suggest two reasons for the shape of this pyramid.

markingPoints.text: high birth rate gives the wide base
high death rate / low life expectancy gives the narrow top
limited access to healthcare or family planning

parts.examinerComment: Link each reason to a feature of the pyramid.

questions.stem: Fig. 3 is a map extract at a scale of 1 : 50 000.

figures.alt: Map extract with grid lines: eastings 20 to 24 and northings 40 to 44. A church symbol is in the middle of the square east of easting 21 and north of northing 43. A school is in the square east of easting 23 and north of northing 40. A river flows west to east.
figures.caption: Fig. 3

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Give the four-figure grid reference of the square containing the church.
parts.examinerComment: Eastings first, then northings.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give the four-figure grid reference of the square containing the school.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Each grid square has sides of 1 km. Estimate the straight-line distance from the church to the school, in km, to 1 decimal place.

markingPoints.text: M1 for measuring or using √(1.9² + 2.9²)
A1 for 3.3 to 3.6 km

parts.examinerComment: Measure between the centres of the symbols.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Students investigate how river velocity changes downstream. Name two pieces of equipment they could use to measure velocity.

markingPoints.text: a float (e.g. dog biscuit or orange)
a stopwatch
a tape measure
a flow meter

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A float travels {d} m in {t} s. Calculate the surface velocity of the river, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: M1 for {d} ÷ {t}
A1 for {=round(d/t, 3)} m/s

parts.examinerComment: Velocity is distance divided by time; some candidates divided time by distance.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Students count pedestrians at five sites in a town. Explain why they should count at the same time of day at each site.

markingPoints.text: pedestrian numbers vary through the day
so the results are comparable / a fair test

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Country X has a birth rate of {b} per 1000 and a death rate of {d} per 1000. Calculate its rate of natural increase as a percentage.

markingPoints.text: M1 for {b} − {d} = {=b-d} per 1000

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates found the natural increase per 1000 but did not convert to a percentage by dividing by 10.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: At the start of a year a town had a population of {p}. During the year there were {bi} births, {de} deaths, {im} immigrants and {em} emigrants. Calculate the population at the end of the year.

markingPoints.text: M1 for {p} + {bi} − {de} + {im} − {em}
A1 for {=p+bi-de+im-em}

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers set out natural change and net migration separately before combining them.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the term for the number of live births per 1000 people in a year.

markingPoints.text: birth rate / crude birth rate

parts.examinerComment: Answers of 'fertility rate' were not credited: that is the average number of children per woman.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Which term describes a country that has too many people for the resources and technology available to support them at a reasonable standard of living?

markingPoints.text: C – overpopulation

parts.examinerComment: Overpopulation depends on resources and technology, not simply on high population density.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Explain why death rates have fallen in many low-income countries in recent decades.

markingPoints.text: Improved health care / more doctors, clinics and hospitals
Vaccination programmes reduce deaths from infectious disease
Cleaner water supply and better sanitation reduce waterborne disease such as cholera
Better nutrition / more reliable food supply
Improved education, e.g. about hygiene and health

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers developed each reason, linking the change to fewer deaths, rather than listing factors.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Give two problems that underpopulation can cause for a country.

markingPoints.text: Shortage of workers / labour, so resources cannot be fully developed
Low tax income to fund services
Services such as schools or hospitals close because of too few users
Small domestic market for businesses

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who confused underpopulation with low density gave weaker answers.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named country you have studied, describe a policy used to influence population growth and evaluate how successful it has been.

markingPoints.text: Country named and policy identified as anti-natalist or pro-natalist
Description of the measures, e.g. limits on family size, free contraception, financial incentives or penalties
Further detail of how the policy was promoted or enforced, e.g. education campaigns, tax benefits, childcare
Evidence of success, e.g. change in birth rate or fertility rate
Limitations or problems, e.g. unpopular, gender imbalance, ageing population, limited effect
Overall judgement of success supported by place-specific detail

parts.examinerComment: Answers that described a policy in general terms with no place-specific detail could not reach full marks. A judgement is needed for the final mark.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how a high birth rate can affect the economic development of a low-income country.

markingPoints.text: Large numbers of young dependants increase spending on education and health
Less money available for investment in industry or infrastructure
Pressure on food, water and housing
Not enough jobs for young people as they reach working age / unemployment

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates described problems without linking them to economic development.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the term for the movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities.

markingPoints.text: rural–urban migration

parts.examinerComment: Urbanisation is the result of this movement, not the movement itself.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which one of the following is a pull factor for a migrant?

options.text: civil war in the home region
lack of health care at home

markingPoints.text: B – better-paid jobs in the destination

parts.examinerComment: Pull factors attract people to the destination; the other options are push factors.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In one year {im} thousand people moved into a country and {em} thousand people left it. Calculate the net migration for that year, in thousands.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=im-em} thousand (negative value means net emigration)

parts.examinerComment: Net migration is immigration minus emigration; a negative answer is valid and shows a net loss.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Define the term refugee.

markingPoints.text: A person forced to leave their home / country
because of persecution, war or natural disaster / fear for their life
and who has crossed an international border

parts.examinerComment: Forced movement is the key idea; 'someone who moves to find work' is an economic migrant.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain the positive and negative impacts of international migration on the destination country.

markingPoints.text: Positive: fills labour shortages, e.g. in health care or farming
Positive: migrants pay taxes / start businesses / cultural diversity
Negative: pressure on housing, schools and health services
Negative: possible tensions with local people / competition for low-paid jobs
Positive: young migrants can offset an ageing population

parts.examinerComment: Both positive and negative impacts are needed for full marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named example of international migration, explain why the migrants left their home country and why they chose their destination.

markingPoints.text: Named source and destination countries
Economic push factors, e.g. unemployment, low wages, poverty
Social or political push factors, e.g. conflict, persecution, poor services
Economic pull factors, e.g. job opportunities, higher wages
Social pull factors, e.g. family links, language, education, safety
Place-specific detail, e.g. numbers, dates, types of job

parts.examinerComment: Generic lists of push and pull factors scored at most four marks. Candidates should use detail from their own case study.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A country has {y} million people aged 0–14, {w} million aged 15–64 and {o} million aged 65 and over. Calculate the dependency ratio, using (young + old dependants) ÷ working population × 100.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round((y+o)/w*100, 1)}

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates forgot to include the elderly dependants.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which feature of a population pyramid shows an ageing population?

options.text: a wide base and a narrow top
a narrow base and a wide top
a wide base that narrows quickly
more males than females at every age

markingPoints.text: B – a narrow base and a wide top

parts.examinerComment: A narrow base shows low birth rates and a wide top shows high life expectancy.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain the problems that a youthful population can cause for a country.

markingPoints.text: High spending needed on schools / education
High demand for health care, e.g. vaccinations, maternal care
Future shortage of jobs as young people reach working age
Pressure on housing and food supply
Large future number of parents so population keeps growing (population momentum)

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained why each demand arises rather than listing services.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Suggest two reasons why women usually outnumber men in the oldest age groups of a high-income country.

markingPoints.text: Women have a higher life expectancy than men
Men more likely to work in dangerous jobs / have had riskier lifestyles, e.g. smoking, alcohol
Men more likely to have died in wars / accidents

parts.examinerComment: Well answered by most candidates.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the term used to describe an area where very few people live.

markingPoints.text: sparsely populated

parts.examinerComment: The opposite term is densely populated.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which one of the following is a human factor that encourages high population density?

options.text: a supply of jobs in industry

markingPoints.text: B – a supply of jobs in industry

parts.examinerComment: The other three are physical factors.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between population distribution and population density.

markingPoints.text: Distribution is the way people are spread out / where people live across an area
Density is the number of people per unit area, e.g. per km²

parts.examinerComment: Many answers defined density well but described distribution only vaguely.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: For a named area of low population density you have studied, explain why few people live there.

markingPoints.text: Named area
Physical factor, e.g. extreme cold or heat, low rainfall
Physical factor, e.g. steep or mountainous relief, thin infertile soils, dense forest
Human factor, e.g. poor accessibility, few jobs, limited services
Each factor linked to why it discourages settlement
Place-specific detail, e.g. temperatures, rainfall figures, density

parts.examinerComment: Answers that simply listed factors without explaining them were limited to three marks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: What is meant by the threshold population of a service?

options.text: the maximum distance people will travel to use it
the minimum number of people needed to support it
the total population of the settlement
the number of people who use it each day

markingPoints.text: B – the minimum number of people needed to support it

parts.examinerComment: Option A describes the range of a good, a common confusion.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Define the range of a good or service.

markingPoints.text: The maximum distance people are willing to travel to buy a good or use a service

parts.examinerComment: Confused with threshold by a number of candidates.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the type of settlement pattern in which buildings are scattered and far apart.

markingPoints.text: dispersed

parts.examinerComment: Nucleated and linear patterns were the most common wrong answers.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A village has a population of {p}. A supermarket chain needs a threshold population of {=p+k} people before it will open a store. How many more people does the village need?

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=p+k} − {p} = {k}

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why many early settlements were built at a wet point site or at a bridging point.

markingPoints.text: Wet point: access to a reliable water supply, e.g. a spring or well
Water needed for drinking, cooking, livestock
Bridging point: a place where the river was shallow / narrow enough to cross
Routes met there so it became a centre for trade

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers explained the advantage of each site rather than simply defining it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why the number of services in many small rural settlements in high-income countries has decreased.

markingPoints.text: Rising car ownership lets people travel to larger centres for shopping
Out-of-town superstores offer lower prices and wider choice
Online shopping reduces demand for local shops
Falling or ageing population means threshold not met
Services close, e.g. village shop, post office, school, bus route

parts.examinerComment: Better answers linked the change to threshold population.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which urban zone in a high-income country typically contains high-density, older terraced housing close to the city centre?

markingPoints.text: B – inner city

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give two reasons why land values are highest in the central business district (CBD).

markingPoints.text: Most accessible location / routes converge there
High demand for limited space / competition for land
Large numbers of potential customers / high footfall

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the term for the process in which run-down inner-city areas are improved when wealthier people move in and renovate housing.

markingPoints.text: gentrification

parts.examinerComment: Urban redevelopment was not credited because it is led by planners rather than residents.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why out-of-town shopping centres are often built on the rural–urban fringe.

markingPoints.text: Cheaper land than in the CBD
Large areas of space for car parking and big stores
Good access from ring roads / motorways
Less congestion than the city centre
Close to large suburban populations

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave the reasons but did not link them to the needs of shopping centres.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For a named urban area you have studied, describe the problems it faces and evaluate the attempts to solve them.

markingPoints.text: Named urban area
Problem described, e.g. traffic congestion, air pollution, housing shortage
Second problem described, e.g. crime, lack of open space, urban sprawl
Solution described, e.g. public transport scheme, new housing, green belt
Evaluation of how effective the solution has been
Place-specific detail, e.g. names of schemes, areas, data

parts.examinerComment: Responses that described problems only, without evaluation, could not reach full marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: In a city, land values fall from US$ {c} per m² at the city centre to US$ {e} per m² at the edge of the city, {d} km away. Calculate the mean fall in land value per km.

markingPoints.text: A1 for US$ {=round((c-e)/d, 1)} per m² per km

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates divided only the city-centre value by the distance.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A country has {u} million people living in urban areas and {r} million living in rural areas. Calculate the percentage of the population that is urban.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round(u/(u+r)*100, 1)} %

parts.examinerComment: The urban population must be divided by the total population, not by the rural population.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which two processes cause the rapid growth of cities in many low-income countries?

markingPoints.text: B – rural–urban migration and natural increase

parts.examinerComment: Both migration and the high natural increase of a youthful urban population contribute.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the term for unregistered and untaxed work, such as street selling or shoe shining, found in many cities in low-income countries.

markingPoints.text: informal sector

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why squatter settlements are often found on steep slopes or on river floodplains.

markingPoints.text: Land is unwanted / not owned or used by others, so less likely to be cleared
These are hazardous sites (landslides, floods) so they were left empty
Often close to jobs in the city / the only free land available

parts.examinerComment: Good answers explained why the land was available, not just that it was dangerous.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain the environmental problems caused by rapid urban growth.

markingPoints.text: Air pollution from traffic and factories, causing respiratory illness
Water pollution from untreated sewage and industrial waste in rivers
Uncollected rubbish / waste dumped in open spaces
Loss of farmland and natural habitats as the city sprawls
Noise pollution / visual pollution

parts.examinerComment: Explanation of the cause of each problem was needed for full marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named city in a low-income or middle-income country, describe the impacts of rapid urban growth on the people who live there.

markingPoints.text: Named city
Housing impacts, e.g. growth of squatter settlements, overcrowding
Service impacts, e.g. lack of clean water, sanitation, electricity
Employment impacts, e.g. unemployment, informal sector work
Health or social impacts, e.g. disease, crime, traffic congestion
Place-specific detail, e.g. named districts, population figures

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers described squatter settlements in general without reference to a specific city.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: At which type of plate boundary does an oceanic plate sink beneath a continental plate?

markingPoints.text: B – destructive (convergent)

parts.examinerComment: At collision boundaries two continental plates meet and neither sinks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the term for the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake.

markingPoints.text: epicentre

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: On the Richter scale each increase of 1 represents a tenfold increase in the amplitude of ground shaking. How many times greater is the amplitude of a magnitude {=b+k} earthquake than a magnitude {b} earthquake?

markingPoints.text: B1 for 10 to the power {k} = {=10^k}

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave the difference in magnitude instead of the multiplying factor.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Describe the structure of the Earth.

markingPoints.text: Crust: thin outer layer, oceanic and continental
Mantle: thick layer of semi-molten rock beneath the crust
Outer core: liquid iron and nickel
Inner core: solid, very hot iron and nickel at the centre

parts.examinerComment: Names of layers with a descriptive point for each were needed.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why earthquakes in low-income countries often cause more deaths than earthquakes of similar strength in high-income countries.

markingPoints.text: Buildings are less likely to be earthquake-resistant / building regulations not enforced
Dense squatter settlements collapse easily
Fewer emergency services / slower rescue
Poor transport links delay aid
Less preparation, e.g. drills, warning systems
Disease spreads afterwards due to lack of clean water and health care

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers made comparisons between the two types of country.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named earthquake or volcanic eruption you have studied, describe its causes and its impacts on people.

markingPoints.text: Named event and location
Plate boundary type identified and plate movement described
Process causing the event explained, e.g. friction and sudden release of pressure, or rising magma
Primary impacts on people, e.g. deaths, injuries, buildings destroyed
Secondary impacts, e.g. homelessness, disease, economic losses, tsunami or lahars
Place-specific detail, e.g. figures, dates, named places

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates wrote a general account of plate tectonics without linking it to their chosen event.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe how the impact of earthquakes can be reduced.

markingPoints.text: Earthquake-resistant buildings, e.g. cross-bracing, rubber foundations, flexible frames
Land-use planning to avoid building on unstable ground
Education and earthquake drills
Emergency kits and well-trained emergency services
Monitoring and warning systems

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which process of erosion occurs when stones carried by a river wear away its bed and banks?

markingPoints.text: B – abrasion

parts.examinerComment: Attrition is the load colliding with itself and becoming smaller and rounder.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the name of the raised bank of deposited material found alongside a river channel, formed when the river floods.

markingPoints.text: levee

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: At a river site the channel is {w} m wide, the mean depth is {d} m and the mean velocity is {v} m/s. Calculate the discharge, in m³/s, using discharge = cross-sectional area × velocity.

markingPoints.text: M1 for {w} × {d} = {=w*d} m² cross-sectional area
A1 for {=round(w*d*v, 3)} m³/s

parts.examinerComment: The cross-sectional area must be found first; some candidates added the values.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Describe how an ox-bow lake forms.

markingPoints.text: Erosion on the outside of a meander bend / deposition on the inside
The neck of the meander becomes narrower
During a flood the river cuts through the neck
The river follows the shorter, straighter course
Deposition seals off the old meander, leaving an ox-bow lake

parts.examinerComment: Diagrams are allowed in the exam; a clear sequence was the key to high marks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain how human activities can increase the risk of river flooding.

markingPoints.text: Urbanisation creates impermeable surfaces so less infiltration
Drains carry water quickly to the river / shorter lag time
Deforestation reduces interception and increases surface run-off
Building on floodplains reduces water storage

parts.examinerComment: Each activity needed a link to more or faster run-off.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named river you have studied, describe the opportunities it offers people and the hazards it creates.

markingPoints.text: Named river
Opportunity, e.g. fertile soils for farming from silt deposits
Opportunity, e.g. water supply, transport, fishing, HEP, tourism
Hazard, e.g. flooding damaging homes and crops
Hazard, e.g. loss of life, disease, erosion of banks
Place-specific detail, e.g. dates of floods, named towns, statistics

parts.examinerComment: Balanced answers covering both opportunities and hazards scored highly.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the type of wave that has a strong backwash and removes material from a beach.

markingPoints.text: destructive wave

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which one of the following is a soft engineering method of coastal management?

markingPoints.text: C – beach nourishment

parts.examinerComment: Groynes are hard engineering structures even though they help to build up the beach.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A cliff top has retreated {d} m in {y} years. Calculate the mean rate of cliff retreat, in m per year.

markingPoints.text: M1 for {d} ÷ {y}
A1 for {=round(d/y, 3)} m per year

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Describe how a headland can be eroded to form a cave, an arch, a stack and a stump.

markingPoints.text: Waves erode lines of weakness, e.g. joints or faults, by hydraulic action and abrasion
A crack is enlarged to form a cave
The cave is eroded through the headland to form an arch
The roof of the arch collapses, leaving a stack
The stack is eroded at its base and collapses to leave a stump

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates named the landforms but did not explain the processes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the conditions needed for coral reefs to grow.

markingPoints.text: Warm water, usually above about 18 °C
Clear water so sunlight reaches the algae
Shallow water, less than about 30 m
Salt water / normal salinity
Little sediment or pollution

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates gave correct conditions but vague values.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why mangroves are valuable to people and the environment.

markingPoints.text: Roots trap sediment and protect the coast from erosion and storm surges
Habitat / nursery for fish and other wildlife
Source of wood, fuel and food for local people
Store carbon / help to reduce climate change

parts.examinerComment: Answers that covered both people and the environment were stronger.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For a named coastline you have studied, describe how it is being managed and evaluate the success of the management.

markingPoints.text: Named coastline
Reason management is needed, e.g. erosion threatening property
Hard engineering method described
Soft engineering or other strategy described
Evaluation: effectiveness, cost, or effects further along the coast
Place-specific detail, e.g. named settlements, costs, dates

parts.examinerComment: Evaluation, including any knock-on effects down-drift, separated the strongest answers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which instrument is used to calculate relative humidity?

markingPoints.text: C – wet and dry bulb thermometer (hygrometer)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Name the instrument used to show wind direction.

markingPoints.text: wind vane

parts.examinerComment: An anemometer measures wind speed, not direction.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the unit used to record cloud cover.

markingPoints.text: oktas

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave percentages, which were not accepted.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A rain gauge recorded {r1}, {r2}, {r3}, {r4} and {r5} mm of rain on five days. Calculate the mean daily rainfall, in mm.
parts.examinerComment: Days with no rain still count when calculating the mean.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe how a rain gauge should be sited and used to give accurate readings.

markingPoints.text: Placed in an open area away from trees and buildings
Sunk into the ground with the rim above the surface to prevent splash-in
Read at the same time each day
Read at eye level in the measuring cylinder
Emptied after each reading

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how a maximum–minimum thermometer records the highest and lowest temperatures since it was last reset.

markingPoints.text: Metal indices (markers) are pushed along the tube by the mercury / liquid
Index stays at the highest point on the maximum side
Index stays at the lowest point on the minimum side
Readings taken from the bottom of the indices, then reset with a magnet

parts.examinerComment: A common error was to suggest that the thermometer records the temperature at a single moment.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which layer of the tropical rainforest forms an almost continuous cover of tree crowns?

markingPoints.text: B – canopy

parts.examinerComment: Emergents stand above the canopy.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why areas with an equatorial climate have high rainfall throughout the year.

markingPoints.text: High sun angle / intense heating all year
Warm air rises (convection) and cools
Water vapour condenses to form cumulonimbus clouds
Heavy convectional rain, often in the afternoon
Low pressure / ITCZ near the equator all year

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers set out the convectional rainfall sequence clearly.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For a named area of tropical rainforest you have studied, explain the causes and impacts of deforestation.

markingPoints.text: Named area
Cause, e.g. logging, cattle ranching, commercial farming
Cause, e.g. mining, roads, HEP schemes, settlement
Environmental impact, e.g. loss of biodiversity, soil erosion
Impact on climate or people, e.g. less transpiration, carbon release, loss of indigenous land
Place-specific detail, e.g. rates of loss, named projects

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who used a named rainforest with specific detail scored the highest marks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A country has a gross national income (GNI) of US$ {g} billion and a population of {p} million. Calculate its GNI per capita, in US$.

markingPoints.text: A1 for US$ {=round(g*1000/p, 1)}

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates lost marks by mishandling billions and millions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which one of the following is a social indicator of development?

markingPoints.text: B – adult literacy rate

parts.examinerComment: Literacy measures education, a social aspect of development.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the term for a company that has its headquarters in one country and operates in several other countries.

markingPoints.text: transnational corporation (TNC)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why infant mortality rate is a useful indicator of development.

markingPoints.text: It reflects the quality of health care / access to doctors and vaccinations
It reflects access to clean water, sanitation and nutrition
It is easy to compare between countries

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to link the indicator to living conditions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain how improvements in transport and communications have encouraged globalisation.

markingPoints.text: Container ships and air freight make it cheaper to move goods around the world
The internet and mobile phones allow instant communication between offices
TNCs can manage factories and supply chains in different countries
Faster travel encourages international business and tourism

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers gave specific examples of technology.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named transnational corporation (TNC) you have studied, describe its global operations and evaluate its impacts on the countries where it has factories or offices.

markingPoints.text: Named TNC and the product or service
Location of headquarters and of factories / branches described
Positive impact, e.g. jobs, training, investment in infrastructure
Positive impact, e.g. tax revenue, multiplier effect, exports
Negative impact, e.g. low wages, poor conditions, profits sent abroad, pollution
Evaluation / overall judgement with place-specific detail

parts.examinerComment: A balanced evaluation with specific detail was needed for six marks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which one of the following is a physical input to a farming system?

markingPoints.text: C – rainfall

parts.examinerComment: Labour, machinery and fertiliser are human inputs.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the type of farming in which both crops and livestock are produced on the same farm.

markingPoints.text: mixed farming

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A farm harvested {t} tonnes of maize from {h} hectares. Calculate the yield, in tonnes per hectare.

markingPoints.text: M1 for {t} ÷ {h}
A1 for {=round(t/h, 3)} t/ha

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how drought can lead to food shortages.

markingPoints.text: Lack of water means crops fail / lower yields
Pasture dies so livestock die or are sold
Less food available so prices rise and the poor cannot afford it
Soil dries out and is eroded, reducing future harvests

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates described drought but did not link it to food supply.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For a named farm or type of agricultural system you have studied, describe its inputs, processes and outputs.

markingPoints.text: Named farm or farming system and location
Physical inputs, e.g. climate, soil, relief
Human inputs, e.g. labour, machinery, seeds, fertiliser, money
Processes, e.g. ploughing, sowing, spraying, harvesting, milking
Outputs, e.g. crops, livestock products, waste
Place-specific detail, e.g. farm size, rainfall, yields

parts.examinerComment: A systems approach, clearly organised into inputs, processes and outputs, helped candidates.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe how high-yielding varieties (HYVs) of crops can increase food supply, and give one disadvantage of using them.

markingPoints.text: HYVs produce larger yields per hectare
Some grow faster, allowing more than one harvest a year
Some are resistant to drought or disease
Disadvantage: need expensive fertiliser, pesticides or irrigation / poorer farmers cannot afford them / loss of crop diversity

parts.examinerComment: The disadvantage was often omitted.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the sector of industry that involves extracting raw materials from the land or sea.

markingPoints.text: primary

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: What is meant by a footloose industry?

options.text: an industry that must locate near its raw materials
an industry that is not tied to a particular location
an industry that relies on unskilled labour
an industry that is located in the informal sector

markingPoints.text: B – an industry that is not tied to a particular location

parts.examinerComment: Footloose industries often use light components and can choose from many locations.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: In a country, {p}% of workers are employed in the primary sector and {s}% in the secondary sector. The rest work in the tertiary and quaternary sectors. Calculate the percentage employed in the tertiary and quaternary sectors.
parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why governments may offer incentives to attract new industries.

markingPoints.text: To create jobs and reduce unemployment
To increase tax income
Multiplier effect: spending supports other businesses
To develop poorer regions / reduce regional inequality
Training raises the skills of the workforce

parts.examinerComment: Some answers described the incentives rather than the reasons for offering them.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For a named factory or industrial zone you have studied, explain the factors that influenced its location.

markingPoints.text: Named factory or zone and location
Physical factor, e.g. flat land, site, water supply
Access to raw materials or components
Labour supply, cost or skills
Transport links / access to markets
Government incentives or place-specific detail

parts.examinerComment: Factors had to be explained, not simply listed, for full marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe the inputs, processes and outputs of a manufacturing industry.

markingPoints.text: Inputs, e.g. raw materials, components, labour, energy, capital
Processes, e.g. assembly, cutting, packaging
Outputs, e.g. finished products, profit, waste

parts.examinerComment: Examples of each part of the system made answers clearer.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Tourist arrivals in a country increased from {a} million to {=a+i} million over five years. Calculate the percentage increase.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round(i/a*100, 1)} %

parts.examinerComment: The increase must be divided by the original value, not the new value.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Which one of the following is a negative environmental impact of tourism?

markingPoints.text: B – footpath erosion

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the term for tourism that aims to conserve the environment and benefit local people.

markingPoints.text: ecotourism

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why not all of the money spent by tourists benefits the local economy.

markingPoints.text: Hotels or tour companies may be owned by foreign TNCs, so profits go abroad (leakage)
Food, drink and goods may be imported
Senior jobs may go to people from outside the area

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers used the term leakage.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain the reasons for the growth of international tourism.

markingPoints.text: Cheaper air travel / budget airlines
Higher incomes / more disposable income
More paid holidays and leisure time
Internet makes booking and research easier
Package holidays and wider range of destinations

parts.examinerComment: Each reason needed development for full marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named area you have studied, describe its attractions for tourists and evaluate the impacts of tourism on it.

markingPoints.text: Named area
Physical attractions described
Human attractions described
Positive economic or social impacts
Negative environmental or social impacts
Evaluation with place-specific detail

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed both description of attractions and a judgement on impacts.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: In one year a country generated {h} TWh of electricity from hydro-electric power, {w} TWh from wind and {f} TWh from fossil fuels. Calculate the percentage of its electricity that came from renewable sources.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round((h+w)/(h+w+f)*100, 1)} %

parts.examinerComment: Both hydro-electric power and wind are renewable.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the fossil fuel formed from the remains of plants that grew in swamps millions of years ago.

markingPoints.text: coal

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Which one of the following is a disadvantage of wind power?

markingPoints.text: B – the supply is not constant

parts.examinerComment: Wind is renewable and does not emit greenhouse gases while generating electricity.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why fuelwood is important in many low-income countries, and describe one problem caused by its use.

markingPoints.text: Free or cheap and available locally
Many rural households lack an electricity or gas supply
Used for cooking and heating
Problem: deforestation / soil erosion / indoor smoke causing respiratory illness / time spent collecting

parts.examinerComment: The problem was often described only vaguely.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why global demand for energy is increasing.

markingPoints.text: Rising world population
Industrialisation in emerging economies
Rising living standards / more electrical goods and cars
Urbanisation increases energy use
Growth in transport and tourism

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers referred to specific countries or regions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named country or area you have studied, describe how one source of energy is used to generate electricity, and evaluate its advantages and disadvantages.

markingPoints.text: Named country or area and energy source
Description of how electricity is generated
Economic advantage, e.g. reliable, cheap running costs, jobs
Environmental advantage or disadvantage
Social or economic disadvantage, e.g. cost, displacement of people, safety
Evaluation with place-specific detail

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates wrote about energy in general and did not name a place.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A town of {p} thousand people uses {v} million litres of water per day for domestic purposes. Calculate the mean domestic water use per person per day, in litres.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round(v*1000/p, 1)} litres

parts.examinerComment: Careful conversion of thousands and millions was needed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Globally, which use accounts for the largest share of fresh water?

markingPoints.text: C – agriculture (irrigation)

parts.examinerComment: Irrigation accounts for roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the term for the removal of salt from sea water to make fresh water.

markingPoints.text: desalination

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how wells and boreholes can provide water, and describe one problem of taking too much groundwater.

markingPoints.text: Wells or boreholes reach water stored in permeable rock (aquifers)
Water pumped to the surface by hand or motor pump
Problem: water table falls so wells dry up
Problem: land subsidence / salt water intrusion near coasts

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why many people in low-income countries do not have access to safe water.

markingPoints.text: Lack of money to build piped supply / treatment works
Rapid urban growth: squatter settlements not connected
Rural areas remote, water must be carried long distances
Water sources polluted by sewage, farming or industry
Drought or low, unreliable rainfall

parts.examinerComment: Both physical and human factors were credited.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named country or area you have studied, describe how the water supply has been increased and evaluate the scheme.

markingPoints.text: Named country or area
Reason more water was needed
Scheme described, e.g. dam, transfer, desalination, wells
Benefits, e.g. reliable supply, irrigation, HEP
Problems, e.g. cost, displacement, environmental damage
Evaluation with place-specific detail

parts.examinerComment: A judgement on the success of the scheme was needed for the top mark.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Which greenhouse gas is released in large amounts by cattle and rice paddies?

markingPoints.text: B – methane

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the term for replanting trees in an area where forest has been cleared.

markingPoints.text: reforestation

parts.examinerComment: Afforestation is planting trees where there was no forest before.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The forest area of a region fell from {a} km² to {=a-l} km² over ten years. Calculate the percentage of the forest that was lost.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round(l/a*100, 2)} %

parts.examinerComment: The loss must be divided by the original area.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain the possible impacts of climate change.

markingPoints.text: Sea-level rise floods low-lying coasts and islands
More frequent extreme weather, e.g. storms, heatwaves, droughts
Changes to crop yields and food supply
Loss of habitats / extinctions, e.g. coral bleaching
Spread of diseases such as malaria to new areas

parts.examinerComment: A wide range of impacts, each explained, scored well.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain how deforestation and overgrazing can lead to soil erosion.

markingPoints.text: Vegetation cover removed so soil exposed to rain and wind
Roots no longer bind the soil
Less interception so more surface run-off washes soil away
Less leaf litter so less humus / soil structure weakens

parts.examinerComment: Clear cause-and-effect chains were needed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For a named area you have studied, describe how economic activity has damaged the environment and evaluate attempts to reduce the damage.

markingPoints.text: Named area and economic activity
Environmental damage described, e.g. pollution, habitat loss
Further damage or its effect on people
Strategy to reduce damage described
Evaluation of strategy's success or limitations
Place-specific detail

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who described damage only could not reach full marks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: On a 1 : 25 000 map, the distance along a road between two junctions is {c} cm. Calculate the real distance, in km.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=c*0.25} km

parts.examinerComment: On a 1 : 25 000 map, 4 cm represents 1 km.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Two villages are {k} km apart. How far apart would they be on a 1 : 50 000 map, in cm?

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=k*2} cm

parts.examinerComment: On a 1 : 50 000 map, 2 cm represents 1 km.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A spot height at the bottom of a valley is {h} m and the summit of a hill is {=h+r} m. The horizontal distance between them is {d} km. Calculate the mean gradient, giving your answer in the form 1 in x (state x only).

markingPoints.text: M1 for vertical interval = {r} m
M1 for horizontal distance = {=d*1000} m
A1 for 1 in {=round(d*1000/r, 1)}

parts.examinerComment: Both distances must be in the same units before dividing.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A farm is on a bearing of 315° from a church. In which direction is the farm from the church?

markingPoints.text: C – north-west

parts.examinerComment: Bearings are measured clockwise from north; 315° is north-west.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A school is on a bearing of 090° from a station. In which compass direction is the school from the station?

markingPoints.text: east

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: On a map with 1 km grid squares, a lake covers {n} complete squares and approximately {hs} half squares. Estimate the area of the lake, in km².

markingPoints.text: B1 for {n} + {hs} ÷ 2 = {=n+hs/2} km²

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: On a map, contours are drawn every 20 m. Point A lies on the 140 m contour and point B lies on the fourth contour above it. State the height of point B, in metres.
parts.examinerComment: Count contour intervals, not contour lines below A.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: In a survey, {a} out of {t} people said they travelled to work by bus. Calculate the percentage who travelled by bus.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=round(a/t*100, 1)} %

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The daily maximum temperatures at a weather station over five days were {t1}, {t2}, {t3}, {t4} and {t5} °C. Calculate the range of these temperatures, in °C.
parts.answerExpression: max(t1, t2, t3, t4, t5) - min(t1, t2, t3, t4, t5)
parts.examinerComment: Range is the highest value minus the lowest; it can be zero if all values are equal.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Which type of graph is most suitable for showing whether there is a relationship between two sets of data?

markingPoints.text: B – scatter graph

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State the name of the straight line drawn on a scatter graph to show the general trend of the points.

markingPoints.text: line of best fit

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Which type of map uses different shades or colours for areas to show values such as population density?

markingPoints.text: A – choropleth map

parts.examinerComment: Isoline maps join points of equal value with lines.

questions.stem:
Table 1 shows data for five countries.

Country | GNI per capita (US$) | Life expectancy (years)
A | 900 | 59
B | 2 400 | 64
C | 8 500 | 71
D | 21 000 | 77
E | 46 000 | 82

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Using Table 1, describe the relationship between GNI per capita and life expectancy.

markingPoints.text: Positive relationship: as GNI per capita increases, life expectancy increases
Data quoted, e.g. country A US$ 900 and 59 years compared with country E US$ 46 000 and 82 years
Life expectancy rises quickly at low incomes and more slowly at higher incomes

parts.examinerComment: Strong answers used paired data from the table to support the trend.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using Table 1, state the difference in life expectancy between country A and country E, in years.

markingPoints.text: 23 years

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Suggest why life expectancy is higher in countries with higher GNI per capita.

markingPoints.text: More money for health care, doctors and hospitals
Better access to clean water and sanitation
Better diet / nutrition
Better education about health

parts.examinerComment: Good answers explained how wealth leads to better health.

questions.stem:
Table 2 shows the population of a city in a middle-income country.

Year | Population (millions)
1980 | 1.2
2000 | 3.0
2020 | 6.6

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Using Table 2, calculate the percentage increase in the city's population between 1980 and 2020.

markingPoints.text: A1 for 450 %

parts.examinerComment: The increase must be divided by the 1980 population.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using Table 2, describe how the rate of the city's population growth changed between 1980 and 2020.

markingPoints.text: Population grew in both periods / more than doubled in each 20-year period
Absolute growth was faster after 2000: 3.6 million compared with 1.8 million
Percentage growth slowed slightly: 150% then 120%

parts.examinerComment: Precise use of data was rewarded.

questions.stem:
Table 3 shows the population and area of three regions.

Region | Population | Area (km²)
P | 360 000 | 1 200
Q | 45 000 | 9 000
R | 1 800 000 | 2 000

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Using Table 3, state which region has the highest population density.

markingPoints.text: R (900 people per km²)

parts.examinerComment: Density must be calculated; R has the largest population and a small area.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using Table 3, calculate the population density of region Q, in people per km².

markingPoints.text: B1 for 5 people per km²

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

questions.stem:
Table 4 shows climate data for a location in a hot desert.

Month | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D
Mean temperature (°C) | 13 | 15 | 19 | 24 | 29 | 33 | 34 | 33 | 30 | 25 | 19 | 14
Rainfall (mm) | 8 | 6 | 4 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 3 | 7

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Using Table 4, calculate the total annual rainfall, in mm.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 30 mm

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using Table 4, calculate the annual temperature range, in °C.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 21 °C

parts.examinerComment: Hot deserts can have a large annual as well as daily range.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe two ways in which plants in hot deserts are adapted to the climate shown in Table 4.

markingPoints.text: Long or wide-spreading roots to reach water
Small, waxy or spiny leaves to reduce transpiration
Thick stems store water, e.g. cacti
Seeds lie dormant until rain, then plants complete life cycle quickly

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to describe the adaptation and link it to the dry climate.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: At 14:00 the dry bulb thermometer read {d} °C and the wet bulb thermometer read {=d-k} °C. Calculate the difference between the two readings, in °C.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {k} °C

parts.examinerComment: A larger difference means lower relative humidity.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A country's population increased from {a} million to {=a+i} million in ten years. Calculate the percentage increase.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round(i/a*100, 1)} %

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Students want to investigate how the number of pedestrians changes with distance from the centre of a town. Write a suitable hypothesis for this investigation.

markingPoints.text: A testable statement linking two variables
e.g. 'Pedestrian numbers decrease as distance from the town centre increases'

parts.examinerComment: Hypotheses written as questions were not credited.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Students interview every tenth person who walks past them. Which sampling method are they using?

markingPoints.text: C – systematic

parts.examinerComment: Systematic sampling selects at regular intervals.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Students time a float over a {d} m stretch of river three times. The times are {t1} s, {t2} s and {t3} s. Calculate the mean velocity, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: M1 for mean time = ({t1} + {t2} + {t3}) ÷ 3 = {=round((t1+t2+t3)/3, 2)} s
M1 for {d} ÷ mean time
A1 for {=round(d/((t1+t2+t3)/3), 3)} m/s

parts.examinerComment: Find the mean time first; averaging three separate velocities gives a slightly different answer.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Name the instrument used to measure the angle of slope of a beach.

markingPoints.text: clinometer

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A river channel is {w} m wide. Depths measured at three equally spaced points across it were {a} m, {b} m and {c} m. Calculate the cross-sectional area, in m², using width × mean depth.

markingPoints.text: M1 for mean depth = ({a} + {b} + {c}) ÷ 3
A1 for {=round(w*(a+b+c)/3, 3)} m²

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates multiplied the width by the deepest point only.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why students should use a pilot study before carrying out their fieldwork.

markingPoints.text: To test that equipment and methods work
To check questionnaire questions are clear
To find practical problems, e.g. safety, timing, access, and adjust the method

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Suggest how students could improve the reliability of a traffic count carried out at five sites.

markingPoints.text: Count at the same time and for the same length of time at each site
Repeat counts on different days and calculate a mean
Use more sites / a larger sample
Avoid unusual days, e.g. market days or bad weather
Use tally charts / more than one counter

parts.examinerComment: Suggestions needed to be practical and linked to reliability.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Describe how students could carry out a questionnaire survey of shoppers to find out how far people travel to a town centre.

markingPoints.text: Choose a sampling method, e.g. systematic every 10th person
Stand at several locations / different times
Ask closed questions, e.g. 'Where have you travelled from?'
Be polite, explain purpose, and record answers on a recording sheet
Aim for a set sample size, e.g. 50 people

parts.examinerComment: Detail on sampling and question design separated stronger answers.

questions.stem:
Table 1 shows pedestrian counts taken for 10 minutes at sites at different distances from a town centre.

Site | Distance from centre (m) | Pedestrians
1 | 0 | 142
2 | 200 | 118
3 | 400 | 96
4 | 600 | 104
5 | 800 | 37

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The hypothesis was 'Pedestrian numbers decrease with distance from the town centre'. To what extent does Table 1 support this hypothesis? Use data in your answer.

markingPoints.text: Largely supports: count falls from 142 at 0 m to 37 at 800 m
General decrease from site 1 to site 3 (142 to 96)
Anomaly: site 4 (104) is higher than site 3 (96)
Suggested reason for anomaly, e.g. a school, bus stop or shop near site 4
Overall conclusion: partly / mostly true

parts.examinerComment: A clear conclusion supported by data and recognition of the anomaly was needed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate the mean number of pedestrians counted per site.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 99.4

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Suggest one way the students could present the data in Table 1, and give a reason for your choice.

markingPoints.text: Scatter graph / line graph of distance against pedestrian count
Shows the relationship / trend with distance clearly
Alternative: proportional symbols on a map, showing location of each site

parts.examinerComment: Pie charts were not suitable for this type of data.
